reason: Pappus can be copious or scanty. The examples are annotated correctly.
The viscidium can be triangular, and the examples agree.
PATO_0000001 'quality' is the generic root. The examples (smooth, toothed, papillose) are surface or margin states and need their own specific terms.
Length of a cauline leaf is meaningful. Some examples include the petiole, which is a minor issue.
A glume can be tapered or narrowed to the apex.
Teeth can be inconspicuous or indistinct.
The epichile can be elliptic, and the examples agree.
A tooth can be conical. 'conic lumens' is a wrong example (it refers to cells), but the pair is valid.
Corona lobes and scales can be linear.
A sepal apex can be cuspidate.
Vein length is meaningful. Some examples describe where the vein arises rather than its length.
PATO_0000001 is the generic quality root. 'entire' and 'serrate' are margin shapes that should use specific terms.
A margin can be velutinous (velvety hairy).
A branch or its bark can be striped or banded.
A leaf lamina can droop or be pendulous.
'lax' and 'laxly arranged' usually describe the inflorescence or spikelets, not the glume. A rule would need the subject of the sentence to be the glume itself.
Flattened applies to many organs, such as stems and fruits, including dorsiventrally flattened ones.
A leaf apex can be sharp or sharply pointed.
Gemmae are counted per cluster or per axil.
An operculum or its beak can be straight.
Cell shape can be rhomboid, as in moss laminal cells.
A raceme can be stiff or inflexible.
Sori can be thick.
Hairiness types (puberulent, villous, hirsute) apply to this anatomy class.
The height of a basal membrane is a valid measurement.
A midvein can protrude. The negated examples ('not projecting') need negation handling, but the pair is valid.
The shape usually belongs to the peristome teeth, not the whole peristome. A rule would need to attach it to 'peristome tooth' when the text says 'teeth'.
Glochids are counted per side or per area.
A compound shape such as lanceolate-triangular is better handled by a rule splitting it into two shapes than by a pair. The examples mix glochids and capsules, and only one flora uses it.
The examples describe a 'spur' (a floral part), not a short shoot. The pair comes from a wrong part reading.
'axillary hyaline nodules' are moss structures, not root nodules, and 'hyaline' is not a quality of a root nodule. The pair rests on a wrong reading.
A margin can be dentate or denticulate.
A flower can be rose coloured.
Lobes and lips can be concave.
Caudicles can be long.
Caudicles can be short.
'Fluted' at the base of a trunk is a furrowed surface. This is acceptable as a stem base shape.
An orchid column can be twisted.
A tuber can be enlarged or large.
A nectary can be elongated.
Operculum length is meaningful. Several examples describe the beak length, which is a minor imprecision.
An ovary can be pulvinate (cushion-like).
An ovary or its apex can be flat.
An ovary can be subovoid.
An ovary can be concealed in the disk.
An ovary can be furrowed (sillonné).
A disk can be circular.
Calyx lobes can be inconspicuous.
Calyx lobes can be undulate.
A raceme can be pedunculate, meaning it has a stalk.
Anther orientation can be oblique or inclined.
A stalk (stipe) can be large or enlarged.
A filament can be setose or setulose. The French 'sétuleux' is slightly finer than setose, a minor imprecision.
An androgynophore has a height.
The length of a pseudopetiole (a leaf base part) is meaningful.
A leaf collar can be smooth.
A leaf epidermis surface can be sericeous (silky).
'capillary' means thin and hair-like, which is a shape. PATO fibrillary means something else, so the pair rests on a wrong reading of the term.
A connective or its appendage can be short.
'Precocious flowering' is about timing (phenology), not growth displacement. A rule would need to map flowering-time words to a phenology term.
